column5: Sketch Map of Track of Expedition
column9: The folding chart at the front of Moss's book, engraved by Marcus Ward and Co. of London and Belfast, showing the outward track of HMS Alert and HMS Discovery in one colour, the homeward track in another and the sledge tracks dotted. It names Floeberg Beach as the Alert's winter quarters, Discovery Harbour as the Discovery's, the farthest reached by Commander Markham and Lieutenant Parr, the farthest reached by Lieutenant Beaumont's sledge party, Cape Britannia, Beaumont Island, Stephenson Island, Mount Hooker, the Polaris winter quarters and Hall's grave, Hayes's Port Foulke, Kane's Rensselaer Bay, the Arctic Highlanders' country south of Cape York, the Crimson Cliffs and the North Water, marked navigable annually. An inset carries the whole run from Davis Strait to Melville Bay.

column5: Plate II: Foulke Fiord and the Inland Ice of Greenland, July 28, 1875
column9: Edward Lawton Moss's chromolithograph of Foulke Fiord in north-west Greenland, its red sandstone walls opening on the white tongue of the inland ice. HMS Alert and HMS Discovery called here on the way north, at the fiord where Isaac Israel Hayes had wintered in 1860-61.

column5: Plate III: Musk Ox Hunt, Discovery Harbour, Midnight, August 25, 1875
column9: Moss's chromolithograph of a musk-ox hunt at midnight in Discovery Harbour: three men with rifles among a small herd, one ox down and bleeding on the snow. It records both how the two ships were fed and the first killing of musk-oxen at Discovery Harbour, six years before Greely's expedition built Fort Conger on the same shore.

column5: Plate IV: Floeberg Beach and the Polar Sea, Looking North from the Crest of Cape Rawson, July, 1876
column9: Moss's chromolithograph from the crest of Cape Rawson: a single figure on the bare red rock of the summit, and beyond him the polar pack running unbroken to the horizon. It is the view that convinced the Nares expedition there was no open polar sea.

column5: Plate V: Winter Quarters Outside, from the Floes Astern of H.M.S. Alert, December, 1875
column9: Moss's chromolithograph of HMS Alert in the polar night at Floeberg Beach, seen from the floes astern: her masts against a brown sky, the housed-over deck glowing, and a man with a lantern crossing the snow toward her. The printed list dates it December 1876; the ship was at Floeberg Beach in the winter of 1875-76 and was home by November 1876.

column5: Plate VI: The Deck: Morning Inspection and Prayers
column9: Moss's chromolithograph of the housed-over upper deck of HMS Alert at Floeberg Beach, the ship's company drawn up in two ranks under the canvas housing for morning inspection and prayers, a hammock and a shovel in the foreground.

column5: Plate VII: Winter Quarters Inside H.M.S. Alert - The Wardroom
column9: Moss's chromolithograph of the Alert's wardroom in winter quarters: three officers at the table under a swinging lamp, pictures and a chart on the bulkhead, a fur rug and the red painted deck. Edward Lawton Moss was the ship's surgeon and painted the room he lived in.

column5: Plate XI: Winter Quarters, from amongst the Floebergs, Looking South, March, 1876
column9: Moss's chromolithograph of two men walking among the floebergs south of the ship in the returning light of March 1876, with the Alert's masts small in the distance and the sun low and yellow behind the ice.

column5: Plate XII: A Floeberg, Simmon's Island, April, 1876
column9: Moss's chromolithograph of the great floeberg at Simmons Island, four sledge-hauliers standing beside its blue-green wall for scale and a loaded sledge behind. Moss describes it in the text: not a large floeberg, but a good example of the structure of polar floe, pushed up the sloping beach until its flat upper surface stood forty feet above the floes around it, the lower half conglomerate ice, the upper stratified white and blue, with a section of a former summer pool in olive-tinted ice overhead and last season's snow on top like sugar on a cake. Position approximate.

column5: Plate XIV: The Most Northern Grave, June, 1876
column9: Moss's chromolithograph of a single wooden headboard on the crest of a snow dome, the floes running away to a dark horizon. It marks the grave of George Porter, a seaman of the Alert who died of scurvy on 8 June 1876 on the return of Albert Hastings Markham's northern sledge party, and it was the northernmost grave in the world when Moss painted it.

column5: Plate XV: Back from the Farthest North
column9: Moss's chromolithograph of Markham's party coming in: five men in harness dragging the boat-sledge over rough floes, the Union Jack and a second flag flying from the sledge, and a man collapsed or resting at the right. Of the fifteen men who went north with Albert Hastings Markham and Alfred Parr, most were down with scurvy by the time they reached the ship, and one, George Porter, did not.

column5: Plate XVI: The Last of the Paleocrystic Floe, Kane's Open Polar Sea, Cape Constitution, Franklin and Crozier Islands in the Distance, August 20, 1876
column9: Moss's final chromolithograph, printed in an engraved border: HMS Alert and HMS Discovery in the pale yellow light of 20 August 1876 as they came south through the last of the old floe, off Cape Constitution with Franklin and Crozier Islands beyond. Moss's own title names the water Kane's Open Polar Sea, which is what Elisha Kent Kane's expedition had claimed to see from this coast in 1854; the Nares expedition had just proved from Cape Rawson that no such sea exists.

Moss's wood-engraved sketch of the ice cave the party found at the head of a ravine near Floeberg Beach, two men standing in the stream that runs through it. Moss describes a roof of white ice streaked with veins of sand and groined into fantastic shapes, an opening overhead letting light through festoons of icicles as thick as a man's body, and sloping shelves of ice over the stream. It is named after a bluejacket of the Discovery's autumn sledge crew who pronounced it a comfortable camping place.
